steps.body:
The calculus in a related-rates problem is three lines. The **hard part is finding the equation**, and nobody hands it to you.

Ask two questions:

**Which quantities are changing?** (label them)
**What ties them together?** (geometry, or a given formula)

And resist the urge to substitute numbers into the picture — a labelled diagram of *variables* is what you want.

explanationVariants: A shadow problem is about SIMILAR TRIANGLES — the lamp, the person and their shadow form two nested right triangles with the same shape.
Pythagoras relates two legs of one right triangle. Similar triangles relate two different triangles, which is what a shadow gives you.

widget.prompt: A person walks away from a lamppost; their shadow lengthens. Which relation should you use?

options.label: Use similar triangles.
options.feedback: Right. The person's height over their shadow equals the lamp's height over the whole base — that proportion IS the relation.

options.label: Use the Pythagorean theorem.
options.feedback: There is no hypotenuse in question here. The link between the distances is a PROPORTION, not a right-angle relation.

options.label: Use the triangle area formula.
options.feedback: Nothing here has an area, and none is asked for. The quantities are LENGTHS, and they are tied together by similarity of the two triangles.

options.label: Use the cone volume formula.
options.feedback: Nothing here is three-dimensional. That relation belongs to the filling-tank problems.

explanationVariants: The ladder's LENGTH never changes, so it is the constant. Both x and y vary, and both pay a d/dt.
Getting this wrong is fatal: differentiating a variable as if it were constant sends its rate to zero.

widget.prompt: For the sliding ladder, which quantities VARY with time?

items.label: x, the foot's distance from the wall
items.feedback: It is being dragged outward at 2 ft/s — that IS its rate of change.

items.label: y, the height on the wall
items.feedback: It falls as x grows. Finding its rate is the whole question.

items.label: The ladder's length, 10 ft
items.feedback: A ladder does not stretch. That is why the right-hand side of the differentiated equation is 0.

items.label: The angle with the ground
items.feedback: It certainly changes — the ladder flattens as it slides. It is simply not the variable this problem asks about.

widget.missFeedback: Ask of each quantity: is it different a second later? If yes, it varies and owes a d/dt.
widget.successFeedback: Only the ladder's length is fixed. Everything else owes a d/dt — and that is exactly why the equation differentiates to zero.

widget.prompt: The cone of water, and where its relation comes from.

panels.title: Two variables, one shape
panels.body: Water fills a cone. The volume depends on BOTH the radius of the surface and the depth: V = (1/3)πr²h. Two unknowns and one equation is not enough.

panels.title: Similar triangles close the gap
panels.body: The cone's shape is fixed, so r and h are locked in proportion — say r = h/2. Substituting gives V in terms of h ALONE: V = (1/12)πh³.

panels.title: Now differentiate
panels.body: dV/dt = (1/4)πh²·(dh/dt). One equation, one unknown rate. The similar triangles were not a trick — they were the step that made the problem solvable at all.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the second panel is the move that unlocks it.
widget.successFeedback: Two variables is one too many. The geometry of the shape supplies the second equation that eliminates one.

steps.body:
Two rules that will save you every time:

**Reduce to one variable BEFORE differentiating.** If your relation has two changing quantities and you only want one rate, use the geometry to eliminate the other first.

**Never put numbers on the diagram.** Label lengths x and h, not 6 and 8. The numbers belong in the last line, and nowhere else.

explanationVariants: With r = h/2, V = (1/3)π(h/2)²h = (1/3)π(h²/4)h = (1/12)πh³ — one variable, ready to differentiate.
Differentiating V = (1/3)πr²h directly would leave both dr/dt and dh/dt in the answer, and you would be stuck.

widget.prompt: V = (1/3)πr²h, and the cone's shape forces r = h/2. What should you differentiate?

options.label: Use V = (1/12)πh³.
options.feedback: Right. Differentiating the two-variable version leaves both dr/dt and dh/dt in your answer, and you cannot finish.

options.label: Use V = (1/3)πr²h.
options.feedback: Then the product rule gives you an equation with TWO unknown rates. Eliminate r first, using the geometry.

options.label: Use only r = h/2.
options.feedback: That is the relation between the variables, not the quantity whose rate you want. Use it to SUBSTITUTE.

options.label: Use V = πr²h.
options.feedback: That is the volume of a CYLINDER. A cone is one third of it — and the relation must be right before any calculus starts.

hints: Two cars, one going north and one going east from the same point — the distance between them is the hypotenuse.
The relation is z² = x² + y², where x and y are the two distances from the junction.
At the instant asked: x = 30, y = 40, so z = 50. Then 2z(dz/dt) = 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt).
explanationVariants: The relation was Pythagoras again — and the whole problem was choosing it and refusing to substitute early.

widget.prompt: Two cars leave a junction, one north at 40 mph and one east at 30 mph. How fast is the distance between them growing when they are 30 and 40 miles out? (mph)

commonErrors.feedback: That is 30 + 40 — but they are travelling at right angles, so the distance grows along the HYPOTENUSE, not the sum. Use z² = x² + y².
That is 40 − 30. The distance is the hypotenuse, and its rate is (30(30) + 40(40))/50 = 50.
That is the average of the two speeds. The correct relation gives dz/dt = 2500/50 = 50 mph.

steps.body: Finding the equation IS the problem.
takeaways: Ask what varies, and what ties them together. Geometry supplies the relation; calculus only differentiates it.
Reduce to one variable BEFORE differentiating, using the shape's fixed proportions.
Label the diagram with variables, never numbers. The numbers belong in the final line.
steps.teaser: Still to come in this course: linearisation, differentials, and L'Hôpital's rule.

concept.body: Before any calculus: what is changing, and what equation ties those things together? Right triangle → Pythagoras. Nested triangles → similar triangles. A solid filling up → its volume formula. Find the equation first; differentiate second.

explanationVariants: Two sides of a right triangle with a fixed hypotenuse: that is Pythagoras.
The fixed hypotenuse is what makes the right-hand side a constant.

widget.prompt: A ladder slides down a wall. Which relation ties its two ends together?

options.label: x² + y² = (ladder length)²
options.feedback: Right — Pythagoras, with a constant on the right because the ladder cannot stretch.

options.label: x + y = ladder length
options.feedback: The ladder is the HYPOTENUSE, not the sum of the legs. Try it with 6, 8 and 10: 6 + 8 is not 10.
